claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed by a dynamic equilibrium between atomic diffusion and surface segregation.
The dynamic equilibrium has a rate constant of 10^-5 s^-1.
The dynamic equilibrium has an activation energy of 1.2 eV.
The relevant diffusion and segregation behavior can be monitored and understood using in situ TEM or XRD.
The initial nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial nanoparticles are 10 nm in diameter.
Atomic diffusion and surface segregation produce a stable surface layer.
The stable surface layer prevents degradation of nanoparticle structure and composition.
A kinetic barrier of 0.5 eV must be overcome for significant atomic diffusion.
In situ characterization and control will increase nanoparticle stability by 20% relative to nanoparticles without characterization and control.
Structural retention is defined as less than 5% deviation in lattice parameter.
Compositional retention is defined as less than 2% deviation in elemental composition.
Nanoparticles containing more than 10% noble metal may exhibit altered stability behavior.
Nanoparticle size and shape may affect stability.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis assigns an activation energy of 1.2 eV, whereas the mechanism assigns a 0.5 eV kinetic barrier to significant diffusion, without distinguishing these as separate processes or barriers.
The intervention includes thermoelectric operation down to 473 K, but the stated overall boundary is 773–1923 K while simultaneously referring to thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K.

In situ TEM or XRD is initially presented as a monitoring method, but the predicted outcome treats characterization and control as a stability-enhancing intervention. No causal route by which observation itself increases stability is specified.
